To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there are many models that simulate the behaviour of surface fire spread, that there are many types of model and that most models are based on empirical data and are therefore limited in the extent of the landscape that they can be used on.
• The most common type of simulation model is a cellular model, in which the fire front is discretised into cells, and the fire spread is calculated for each individual cell.
• The most common mathematical analogue fire models are those that assume that a fire spreads as a circle, ellipse or paraboloid.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of models of wildland fire behaviour and spread.

the following issues: (1) What are the key issues in the modelling of wildland fire? (2) What are the different types of model? (3) What are the strengths, weaknesses, and limitations of each type of model? and (4) How can the modelling of wild land fire be improved in the future?

the development of models that can be applied at landscape scales and are capable of representing the complex interactions of fire with the landscape, including fire spread, fire intensity, fire behaviour, fire effects, and the impacts of prescribed fire on fuels, vegetation and wildlife.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, despite the many advances and developments in fire modelling over the past 10-15 years, there is no single model that has been shown to be superior to any other in terms of accuracy, reliability, and ease of application.
there is no single model that adequately simulates the spread and behaviour of wildland fires over a landscape.
the models discussed in this paper have limited application and are not generally recommended.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the models developed since 2005 are more comprehensive, more flexible, more accurate, more realistic, and better able to incorporate spatially explicit data than those developed before 2005.
there is a wide range of simulation models, but that most are limited in their application to specific types of fuels, topographies, and weather conditions.
, in the past 20 years, the number of fire spread models has grown exponentially and there is now a bewildering array to select from.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are many different types of model and many different approaches to model development.
the vast majority of models are not validated against empirical data and are not suitable for predicting fire spread.
the vast majority of models have a limited spatial resolution and that most models are not able to capture the complexity of fire spread across the landscape.
